# Crossing, Decaying Resonances, and Quantum Tunnelling in $a_r^{(1)}$ {#sec-lec5-crossing-resonances}

> **Companion reading in the book:** the chapters [Sine-Gordon and sinh-Gordon with a defect](book:sec-defect-sine-gordon) and [Soliton transmission matrices](book:sec-soliton-transmission).

In Lecture 4 (@sec-lec4-quantum-groups), we solved the linear Borel intertwining equations for sine-Gordon ($a_1^{(1)}$) and found that they uniquely determine the operator matrix structure of the soliton transmission matrix $\mathbb{T}(\theta)$ up to a single scalar factor $\Phi(\theta)$:
$$
\mathbb L(\theta)=P\mathbb T(\theta)=\Phi(\theta)
\begin{pmatrix}W^{-1}&-iY\,U^{-1}q^sW\\-iY\,UW^{-1}&q^sW\end{pmatrix},
\qquad Y=e^{\lambda(\theta-\theta_d)}.
$$ {#eq-lec5-sg-t-reminder}

Now comes the physical heart of the quantum bootstrap: **how do we determine the overall scalar factor $\Phi(\theta)$, what poles does it introduce in the complex $\theta$-plane, and what happens when we generalize from $a_1^{(1)}$ to the higher-rank necklace $a_r^{(1)}$ (such as $a_2^{(1)}$)?**

In this lecture, we will do three crucial calculations on the blackboard that every student of integrable field theory should master:

1. **Unitarity, Crossing, and How Crossing Fixes the Physical Sign of $q$:**
   We will invert $\mathbb{T}(-\theta)$ on each 2-dimensional charge sector $\{v_+ \otimes |n\rangle, v_- \otimes |n+1\rangle\}$ to obtain the right-to-left transmission matrix $\bar{\mathbb{T}}(\theta) = \mathbb{T}(-\theta)^{-1}$, and impose the defect crossing relation $\bar{\mathbb{T}}_{a\alpha}^{b\beta}(\theta) = C_{aa'}\mathbb{T}_{b'\alpha}^{a'\beta}(i\pi - \theta)C^{b'b}$. In the process, we will see a striking algebraic miracle: **the four matrix entries of the crossing equation are mutually consistent precisely at the physical sign in our fixed charge-conjugation convention**
   $$
   q = -e^{-i\pi\lambda} = e^{-\frac{8\pi^2 i}{\beta_{\rm SG}^2}},\qquad \lambda=\frac{8\pi}{\beta_{\rm SG}^2}-1.
   $$
   At the unphysical sign $+e^{-i\pi\lambda}$, the diagonal and off-diagonal entries of crossing demand opposite signs for $\Phi(\theta)\Phi(\theta + i\pi)$!
2. **The Infinite Gamma-Product Scalar Factor, Wigner's Time Delay, and the Unstable Resonance:**
   We will solve the functional equations for $\Phi(\theta)$ using an infinite product of Gamma functions, verify that its semiclassical $(\lambda \to \infty)$ phase derivative reproduces the classical Hirota soliton delay $\ln\left|\coth\frac{\theta-\theta_d}{2}\right|$ via Wigner's time-delay formula, and analyze the resonance pole at $\theta_P = \theta_d - \frac{i\pi}{2\lambda}$, showing how the defect bootstrap on the rank-1 residue produces the **excited odd-sector defect** ($s = 1$, $\theta_d \mapsto \theta_d - i\pi$).
3. **The $a_2^{(1)}$ Soliton Transmission Matrices and Quantum Tunnelling:**
   We will construct the $a_r^{(1)}$ root-lattice Weyl module $\mathcal{W}$ and derive the transmission matrices $M_V(\theta)$ (for the fundamental triplet $V = \mathbf{3}$) and $M_{\bar{V}}(\theta)$ (for the antitriplet $\bar{V} = \bar{\mathbf{3}}$) both by solving the $U_q(\mathfrak{b}^-)$ intertwining relations and by fusing two $V$-solitons via the defect bootstrap. This calculation reveals a jewel of quantum integrability: while $M_V(\theta)$ has only **two** non-zero transitions per state (obeying the classical chiral selection rule of Lecture 3), $M_{\bar{V}}(\theta)$ has **all three** transitions non-zero—exhibiting **quantum tunnelling** into the classically forbidden topological charge sector near $\theta \approx \theta_d$, which vanishes exponentially in the classical limit $\omega \to \infty$!

---

## Unitarity, Crossing, and How Crossing Fixes the Sign of $q$ {#sec-lec5-unitarity-crossing}

Use the ordered bases $v_+\otimes|n\rangle,v_-\otimes|n+1\rangle$ on the incoming charge sector and $|n\rangle\otimes v_+,|n+1\rangle\otimes v_-$ on the outgoing sector. The corresponding matrix is
$$
\mathbb T_n(\theta)=\Phi(\theta)
\begin{pmatrix}q^{-n}&-iYq^{n+1+s}\\-iYq^{-n}&q^{n+1+s}\end{pmatrix}
=\Phi(\theta)\begin{pmatrix}1&-iY\\-iY&1\end{pmatrix}
\operatorname{diag}(q^{-n},q^{n+1+s}).
$$ {#eq-lec5-tn-2x2}
Its determinant is
$$
\det\mathbb T_n(\theta)=\Phi(\theta)^2q^{1+s}(1+Y^2).
$$ {#eq-lec5-det-tn}
The factor $q^{1+s}$ is independent of $n$. In particular, every block has rank one when $Y=\pm i$, provided the scalar factor is removed before taking this limit.

### Step 1: Defect Unitarity and $\bar{\mathbb T}(\theta)$

Defect unitarity defines the reverse transmission by $\bar{\mathbb T}(\theta)=\mathbb T(-\theta)^{-1}$. Put $Z=Y(-\theta)$ in this subsection. Direct inversion gives
$$
\bar{\mathbb T}_n(\theta)=\frac1{\Phi(-\theta)(1+Z^2)}
\begin{pmatrix}q^n&iZq^n\\iZq^{-n-1-s}&q^{-n-1-s}\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-lec5-tbar-from-unitarity}
For real $\theta,\theta_d,\lambda,s$ and $|q|=1$, the diagonal matrix of $q$-powers is unitary, while
$\big(\begin{smallmatrix}1&iY\\iY&1\end{smallmatrix}\big)
\big(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-iY\\-iY&1\end{smallmatrix}\big)=(1+Y^2)1$.
Thus Hermitian unitarity is exactly
$$
|\Phi(\theta)|^2(1+e^{2\lambda(\theta-\theta_d)})=1.
$$ {#eq-lec5-phi-unitarity-real}
The reverse scalar factor is
$$
\bar\Phi(\theta)=\frac1{\Phi(-\theta)(1+Y(-\theta)^2)}.
$$ {#eq-lec5-bar-phi}
This definition follows from matrix inversion. It is not an analytic continuation of a complex-conjugation identity with $\theta$ replaced by $-\theta$.

### Step 2: Defect Crossing and the Sign of $q$

The charge-conjugation matrix is $C=\sigma_x$. In particle indices, with the defect labels kept fixed, crossing is
$$
\bar{\mathbb T}_{a\alpha}^{b\beta}(\theta)
=C_{aa'}\mathbb T_{b'\alpha}^{a'\beta}(i\pi-\theta)C^{b'b}.
$$ {#eq-lec5-crossing-eq}
This is a partial transpose in the particle indices. It is not the transpose of a single charge block: conjugation changes which charge block an entry belongs to.

For the diagonal process $(+,n)\to(+,n)$, the inverse gives
$q^n/[\Phi(-\theta)(1+Z^2)]$, while the crossed process is $(-,n)\to(-,n)$, with amplitude $\Phi(i\pi-\theta)q^{n+s}$. Hence
$$
\Phi(-\theta)\Phi(i\pi-\theta)(1+Z^2)=q^{-s}.
$$ {#eq-lec5-crossing-diag}
For the converting process $(+,n)\to(-,n+1)$, compare the bottom-left entry of the inverse with the same converting entry of the crossed matrix:
$$
\frac{iZq^{-n-1-s}}{\Phi(-\theta)(1+Z^2)}
=-i\Phi(i\pi-\theta)e^{i\pi\lambda}Zq^{-n}.
$$ {#eq-lec5-offdiag-lhs}
Using the diagonal condition reduces this equation to
$$
q^{-1}=-e^{i\pi\lambda},\qquad
Y(\theta+i\pi)=-q^{-1}Y(\theta).
$$ {#eq-lec5-y-shift-q}
The second diagonal and converting processes give the same conditions. Replacing $-\theta$ by $\theta$ yields
$$
\Phi(\theta)\Phi(\theta+i\pi)(1+e^{2\lambda(\theta-\theta_d)})=q^{-s}.
$$ {#eq-lec5-master-crossing-phi}
All four entries, including their shifted defect labels, are checked in `code/lectures/gemini_l45_verified.py`.

With the same displayed matrix and $C=\sigma_x$, changing to $q=+e^{-i\pi\lambda}$ makes the off-diagonal condition incompatible with the diagonal one. This selects the minus sign in these exchange conventions. It is not a convention-independent obstruction: a Klein-factor change also changes the bulk exchange rules and the crossing pairing. For a real offset $s$, multiplying the $s=0$ scalar solution by $q^{-s/2}$ gives the required right-hand side and preserves its modulus.

## The Gamma-Product Scalar Factor, Semiclassical Delay, and the Decaying Resonance {#sec-lec5-gamma-and-resonance}

Let us solve (-@eq-lec5-master-crossing-phi) (for the fundamental even defect $s = 0$, setting $\hat{\theta} = \theta - \theta_d$ and $Y = e^{\lambda\hat{\theta}}$):
$$
\Phi(\hat{\theta})\,\Phi(\hat{\theta} + i\pi) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{2\lambda\hat{\theta}}} = \frac{1}{(1 + i e^{\lambda\hat{\theta}})(1 - i e^{\lambda\hat{\theta}})}.
$$ {#eq-lec5-phi-func-eq}

### Solving the Functional Equation via Infinite Gamma Products

Write $u=\theta-\theta_d$. The even-sector minimal solution has the Gamma-product form [@konik_leclair1999; @bcz2005]
$$
\Phi(\theta)=\frac{e^{i\pi(1+\lambda)/4}}{1+ie^{\lambda u}}
\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{r_N(u)}{\bar r_N(u)},
$$ {#eq-lec5-phi-gamma}
where
$$
r_N(u)=\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}
\frac{\Gamma(k\lambda+\frac14-\frac{i\lambda u}{2\pi})
\Gamma((k+1)\lambda+\frac34-\frac{i\lambda u}{2\pi})}
{\Gamma((k+\frac12)\lambda+\frac14-\frac{i\lambda u}{2\pi})
\Gamma((k+\frac12)\lambda+\frac34-\frac{i\lambda u}{2\pi})}.
$$
The bar changes $i$ to $-i$ in the Gamma arguments without conjugating $u$. The cutoff is common to both products. The constant phase in (-@eq-lec5-phi-gamma) is required by the crossing normalization; it is not optional.

For real $u$, $r_N/\bar r_N$ has modulus one, so unitarity is immediate. To check crossing, shift $u\mapsto u+i\pi$ in the Gamma arguments and use $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)=\pi/\sin\pi z$, retaining the endpoint factors before taking the limit. Each product separately grows as $N^{(\lambda+1)/4}$, but the ratio of the $k$-th factors differs from one by $O(k^{-2})$, so the common-cutoff ratio converges. The [book's scalar-factor section](book:sec-sg-transmission-matrix) gives its equivalent integral representation. `code/lectures/gemini_l45_verified.py` evaluates this product independently, checks the crossing normalization and checks the pole orders below. `code/defect_sg_transmission.py` provides the book's implementation.

### Semiclassical Limit and Wigner's Time Delay

Let us check that our quantum scalar factor (-@eq-lec5-phi-gamma) knows about our classical Bäcklund calculation from Lecture 2! In the classical limit $\beta \to 0$, the coupling parameter $\lambda = \frac{8\pi}{\beta_{\rm SG}^2} - 1 \to \infty$. By Wigner's semiclassical time-delay relation, the derivative of the quantum transmission phase $\Theta(\hat{\theta}) = \arg\Phi(\hat{\theta})$ with respect to rapidity must reproduce the logarithm of the classical Hirota spatial shift $|z_{\text{I}_-}(\theta)| = \left|\coth\frac{\theta - \theta_d}{2}\right|$:
$$
\lim_{\lambda \to \infty} \frac{\pi}{\lambda + 1}\frac{d}{d\theta}\arg\Phi(\theta - \theta_d) = \ln\!\left|\coth\!\left(\frac{\theta - \theta_d}{2}\right)\right|!
$$ {#eq-lec5-wigner-delay}
One way to see the classical limit is to differentiate the integral representation of the scalar phase. For real $u$ it gives
$$
\frac{d}{du}\arg\Phi(u)
=\int_0^\infty\frac{\tanh(\pi k/2)\cos(ku)}{2\sinh(\pi k/(2\lambda))}\,dk.
$$
The large-$\lambda$ limit of the scaled integral, at fixed $u\ne0$, has the convergent expansion
$$
2\sum_{j=0}^\infty\frac{e^{-(2j+1)|u|}}{2j+1}
=\log\frac{1+e^{-|u|}}{1-e^{-|u|}}
=\log\left|\coth\frac u2\right|.
$$
The logarithm follows by subtracting the two power series for $\log(1\pm e^{-|u|})$. The limit is nonuniform at $u=0$, where the classical delay diverges. The numerical convergence is shown in @fig-lec5-resonance-wigner.

### The Resonance Pole and the Excited Odd Defect ($s = 1$)

The factor $(1+ie^{\lambda u})^{-1}$ has a simple pole at $u_+=i\pi/(2\lambda)$. But at this point the $k=0$ numerator factor of $\bar r_N$ is
$\Gamma(\frac14+\frac{i\lambda u_+}{2\pi})=\Gamma(0)$.
Thus $1/\bar r_N$ has a simple zero and cancels the apparent upper pole. At $u_-=-i\pi/(2\lambda)$ it is the numerator of $r_N$ that has the Gamma pole, while $1+ie^{\lambda u_-}=2$. The nearest lower pole therefore survives:
$$
\theta_P=\theta_d-\frac{i\pi}{2\lambda}.
$$ {#eq-lec5-resonance-pole}

What is the physics of a pole at $\theta_P = \theta_d - \frac{i\pi}{2\lambda}$ in the lower half-plane $\operatorname{Im}\theta < 0$? Let us compute the energy of the composite system (defect + soliton at rapidity $\theta_P$):
$$
\Delta E = M\cosh\theta_P = M\cosh\!\left(\theta_d - \frac{i\pi}{2\lambda}\right) = \underbrace{M\cosh\theta_d \cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2\lambda}\right)}_{\operatorname{Re}\Delta E} - i\underbrace{M\sinh\theta_d \sin\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2\lambda}\right)}_{\Gamma/2}!
$$ {#eq-lec5-resonance-energy}
For $\theta_d > 0$ and $\lambda > 1/2$, the imaginary part is negative ($\Gamma = 2M\sinh\theta_d\sin\frac{\pi}{2\lambda} > 0$), which is the hallmark of an **unstable decaying resonance** with lifetime $\tau = 1/\Gamma$! (Recall from Lecture 2 that for $\theta_d > 0$, a classical soliton at $\theta = \theta_d > 0$ moves to the right and can be absorbed/emitted at $x=0$; in the quantum theory, this marginal classical absorption at $\theta = \theta_d$ shifts down to $\theta_P = \theta_d - \frac{i\pi}{2\lambda}$ and acquires a quantum decay width $\Gamma$!)

And what happens when we apply the **defect bootstrap** (@eq-lec1-defect-bootstrap from Lecture 1) at the pole $\theta_P = \theta_d - \frac{i\pi}{2\lambda}$? At $\theta = \theta_P$, $e^{\lambda(\theta_P - \theta_d)} = -i$, so the $2\times 2$ matrix in (-@eq-lec5-tn-2x2) has determinant $1 + (-i)^2 = 0$ and rank 1! Projecting onto the 1-dimensional residue image in each charge sector $\mathcal{H}_n$ shifts the Weyl module parameter from $s = 0$ to $s = 1$ and shifts $\theta_d \mapsto \theta_d - i\pi$, producing the **odd-sector sine-Gordon defect**! Both the physical-strip pole cancellation at $+\frac{i\pi}{2\lambda}$ versus the resonance pole at $-\frac{i\pi}{2\lambda}$ and the semiclassical Wigner delay convergence (-@eq-lec5-wigner-delay) are shown in @fig-lec5-resonance-wigner (`code/lectures/gemini_l5_f1_resonance_wigner.py`).

![Analytic structure and semiclassical limit of the sine-Gordon scalar factor $\Phi(\theta - \theta_d)$: (a) along the imaginary axis $\theta - \theta_d = i\eta$, the bare pole of $(1 + i e^{\lambda u})^{-1}$ at $\eta = +\frac{\pi}{2\lambda}$ in the physical strip is cancelled by the zero of $1/\bar{r}(i\eta)$, leaving only the lower half-plane resonance pole at $u_P = -\frac{i\pi}{2\lambda}$; (b) Wigner's quantum time delay $\frac{\pi}{\lambda+1}\frac{d}{d\theta}\arg\Phi(\theta-\theta_d)$ converging to the classical Bäcklund delay $\ln|\coth\frac{\theta-\theta_d}{2}|$ as $\lambda \to \infty$.](figures/l5_resonance_wigner.svg){#fig-lec5-resonance-wigner width=92% fig-alt="Two-panel plot showing physical-strip pole cancellation at +i*pi/(2*lambda) and the decaying resonance pole at -i*pi/(2*lambda) in panel (a), and convergence of the quantum Wigner time delay to the classical Bäcklund delay ln|coth((theta-theta_d)/2)| in panel (b)."}

## The $a_2^{(1)}$ Soliton Transmission Matrices and Quantum Tunnelling {#sec-lec5-a2-tunnelling}

Now let us move from $a_1^{(1)}$ to the higher-rank necklace $a_r^{(1)}$ ($h = r+1$), focusing on our showcase multi-component laboratory **$a_2^{(1)}$ ($r = 2, h = 3$)**!

In $a_2^{(1)}$, there are two soliton multiplets:
- The fundamental **vector soliton** $V = \mathbf{3}$ ($a = 1$, mass $M_1 = \frac{12m}{\beta^2}\sin\frac{\pi}{3}$), with basis $\{|1\rangle_V, |2\rangle_V, |3\rangle_V\}$ corresponding to the three weights of the fundamental representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_3$.
- The conjugate **antivector soliton** $\bar{V} = \bar{\mathbf{3}}$ ($a = 2$, mass $M_2 = M_1$), with basis $\{|\bar{1}\rangle_{\bar{V}}, |\bar{2}\rangle_{\bar{V}}, |\bar{3}\rangle_{\bar{V}}\}$, which is the bound state of two $V$-solitons at the fusing angle $\theta_{12} = \frac{2\pi i}{3}$ ($V \wedge V \simeq \bar{V}$).

### Constructing the Root-Lattice Weyl Module $\mathcal{W}$ for $a_r^{(1)}$

Write $h=r+1$ and use orthonormal coordinate vectors $e_i$ in $\mathbb R^h$, with indices understood cyclically. The roots are $\alpha_j=e_j-e_{j+1}$, including $\alpha_h=\alpha_0$. Label the defect by
$$
|N\rangle,\qquad N\in\mathbb Z^h,\qquad \sum_iN_i=0,
$$
and fix an offset $s\in\mathbb R^h$ with $\sum_i s_i=0$. There are $r$ independent integer labels. The stored charge is $N+s$.

Set $\omega=4\pi/\beta^2-1$, $q=-e^{-i\pi\omega}$, $y=e^{\omega\theta}$, $y_d=e^{\omega\theta_d}$ and $\mu=-e^{-i\pi\omega/2}/(q-q^{-1})$. The lower Borel acts by
$$
\rho(k_j)|N\rangle=q^{\alpha_j\cdot(N+s)}|N\rangle,\qquad
\rho(f_j)|N\rangle=\frac\mu{y_d}q^{(N+s)_{j+1}}|N-\alpha_j\rangle.
$$ {#eq-lec5-ar-weyl-action}
The Cartan relation follows because lowering $N$ by $\alpha_j$ multiplies the $k_i$ eigenvalue by $q^{-\alpha_i\cdot\alpha_j}$. Also, $f_{j+1}$ lowers the $(j+1)$-th component of $N$ by one. Therefore
$$
f_jf_{j+1}=q^{-1}f_{j+1}f_j.
$$ {#eq-lec5-fj-clock}
For a neighbouring pair this implies the cubic $q$-Serre relation: after moving $f_{j+1}$ to the left, its coefficient is $q^{-2}-(q+q^{-1})q^{-1}+1=0$. Non-neighbouring generators commute. These calculations explain both the root shift and the $q$-power in the module.

### The Vector and Antivector Matrices

Let $X=e^{\omega(\theta-\theta_d-i\pi/2)}=-(q-q^{-1})\mu y/y_d$. In the vector representation, $f_jv_j=y^{-1}v_{j+1}$; in the conjugate representation, $f_j\bar v_{j+1}=y^{-1}\bar v_j$. The Cartan weights are respectively $e_i-\frac1h\sum_k e_k$ and its negative.

::: {#prp-lec5-a2-matrices}
**[Established]** **The $a_r^{(1)}$ vector and antivector transmission matrices.**
In the chosen Weyl basis, the matrix parts of the type-I$_-$ transmission operators are
$$
M_V(v_i\otimes|N\rangle)=q^{-(N+s)_i}|N\rangle\otimes v_i
+X|N+e_i-e_{i-1}\rangle\otimes v_{i-1},
$$ {#eq-lec5-a2-t1}
$$
M_{\bar V}(\bar v_i\otimes|N\rangle)
=\sum_{j=0}^{h-1}X^j q^{\sum_{k=0}^j(N+s)_{i+k}}
|N-e_i+e_{i+j}\rangle\otimes\bar v_{i+j}.
$$ {#eq-lec5-a2-t2}
Scalar factors multiply these matrix parts. These are the conventions of [the book](book:prp-an-transmission), corresponding to Corrigan and Zambon [@cz2009a].
:::

Each branch preserves total charge. For example, the converting vector branch replaces $e_i$ by $e_{i-1}$ and adds $e_i-e_{i-1}$ to the defect. Substitution into the coproduct equation verifies the coefficients; `code/lectures/gemini_l45_verified.py` performs the independent sparse-action check for $h=3,4,5$.

For $a_2^{(1)}$, the vector has two branches, $i\to i$ and $i\to i-1$. The antivector has three, labelled by $j=0,1,2$. It can also be obtained by fusing two vectors at rapidities $\theta\pm i\pi/3$:
$$
M_{\bar V}(\theta)\propto
\Pi_{\bar V}M_{V_1}(\theta-i\pi/3)M_{V_2}(\theta+i\pi/3)\iota_{\bar V}.
$$ {#eq-lec5-vbar-from-fusion}
Here $\iota_{\bar V}$ and $\Pi_{\bar V}$ are the bulk fusion inclusion and projection, with the tensor ordering fixed by the defect bootstrap. The explicit matrices, rather than just counting two successive steps, determine the surviving branches.

For real rapidities and offsets the three antivector amplitudes have relative moduli $1,|X|,|X|^2$. The classical rule permits the $j=0$ and $j=2$ endpoints. The intermediate branch obeys
$$
\frac{|M_{j=1}|}{\max(|M_{j=0}|,|M_{j=2}|)}
=\min(|X|,|X|^{-1})=e^{-\omega|\theta-\theta_d|}.
$$
It is exponentially suppressed at fixed $\theta\ne\theta_d$ as $\omega\to\infty$, while all three moduli coincide at $\theta=\theta_d$. This is the extra quantum transition usually called tunnelling [@cz2007; @cz2010]. It concerns the algebraic scattering solution. Identifying that solution with the quantum Lagrangian defect remains a separate conjecture; see [the book's Lagrangian caveat](book:sec-t-procedure).

Finally, just as in sine-Gordon, unitarity and crossing between $M_V(\theta)$ and $M_{\bar{V}}(\theta)$ (see the book: [equation](book:eq-dt-crossing), [Crossing and the scalar factor](book:prp-transmission-crossing)) fix the overall scalar factor $g(\theta)$ (see [the book](book:eq-dt-g)) as an infinite Gamma-function product, and its poles in the complex $\theta$-plane produce a discrete window of unstable defect–soliton bound states whose number depends on the coupling $\omega$ (see the book: [equation](book:eq-dt-window), [Unstable states of the $a_2$ defect](book:prp-a2-unstable)). The illustrative values $\omega=1.2,4.5$ in the weight plot evaluate only the scalar powers $|X|^{2j}$; all representation checks use irrational $\omega$. Both the three-branch quantum tunnelling weights of $M_{\bar{V}}(\theta)$ and the $a_2^{(1)}$ resonance stability windows are plotted in @fig-lec5-a2-tunnelling (`code/lectures/gemini_l5_f2_a2_tunnelling.py`).

![Multi-branch quantum tunnelling and resonance windows in $a_2^{(1)}$ ($h=3$): (a) normalized branch weights $p_j(\theta) = |X|^{2j}/(1 + |X|^2 + |X|^4)$ ($j=0,1,2$) for $\bar{V}$ at $\omega = 1.2$ versus $\omega = 4.5$, showing the $j=1$ quantum tunnelling peak $p_1(\theta_d) = 1/3$ and its exponential suppression $\propto e^{-2\omega|\theta-\theta_d|}$ away from $\theta_d$; (b) resonance pole trajectories $\operatorname{Im}(\theta_a - \theta_d)/\pi = \frac{1}{2} - (\frac{3-a}{3} + \frac{1}{3\omega})$ against $1/\omega$, highlighting the decaying-resonance windows $\frac{1}{\omega} \in (0, 1)$ for $V$ ($a=1$) and $\frac{1}{\omega} \in (\frac{1}{2}, 2)$ for $\bar{V}$ ($a=2$).](figures/l5_a2_tunnelling.svg){#fig-lec5-a2-tunnelling width=92% fig-alt="Two-panel plot showing the three normalized branch weights p_0, p_1, p_2 of anti-soliton Vbar transmission in a_2^(1) with the j=1 quantum tunnelling peak in panel (a), and the resonance pole trajectories Im(theta_a - theta_d)/pi versus 1/omega in panel (b)."}

## Exercises for Lecture 5

::: {#exr-lec5-omega-trick}
**The Quadratic $\Omega_j$ Trick on $V \otimes \mathcal{W}$ and $\bar{V} \otimes \mathcal{W}$.**
Use $\Delta(f_j)=f_j\otimes k_j^{-1}+1\otimes f_j$ and (-@eq-lec5-fj-clock) to expand
$$
\Omega_j=\Delta(f_j)\Delta(f_{j+1})-q^{-1}\Delta(f_{j+1})\Delta(f_j).
$$
Show that the term acting on the defect alone vanishes and the remaining terms are
$$
(f_jf_{j+1}-q^{-1}f_{j+1}f_j)\otimes k_j^{-1}k_{j+1}^{-1}
+(q-q^{-1})f_{j+1}\otimes k_{j+1}^{-1}f_j.
$$
Use the vector and antivector actions above to determine its image and kernel on a fixed total-charge sector. Explain how an endomorphism commuting with all $\Omega_j$ is forced to preserve the corresponding coordinate lines or hyperplanes.
:::

::: {#exr-lec5-odd-defect-bootstrap}
**Bootstrapping the Odd Sine-Gordon Defect ($s=1$) at $\theta_P = \theta_d - \frac{i\pi}{2\lambda}$.**
Strip off $\Phi$ before taking the residue limit. At $Y(\theta_P)=-i$, show that the matrix part in (-@eq-lec5-tn-2x2) has image spanned, in the outgoing basis, by
$$
|n\rangle\otimes v_+-|n+1\rangle\otimes v_-.
$$
Use the defect bootstrap with the bulk sine-Gordon S-matrix to restrict transmission to these image lines. Compare the resulting matrix with the odd-sector Weyl matrix after a diagonal change of basis, as in [the book](book:sec-sg-defect-spectrum). Why is substituting $\theta_P$ into the full, singular $\mathbb T$ different from computing the image of its residue?
:::
